human-rights-epistemological-basis.title: What grounds human rights?
human-rights-epistemological-basis.lede: Modern human rights are often treated as a universal moral truth. The paper argues they rest on secular Enlightenment assumptions, and questions whether that foundation is as universal as claimed.
body: Human rights are often presented as the moral framework of the modern world, something every culture should accept. The authors ask where that framework actually comes from, and what it assumes about human beings, morality and religion. Their argument is that it is not neutral: it grew out of a particular history and carries a particular view of what a human being is.

Their answer is historical. The paper traces modern human rights through the Renaissance and Reformation, the Enlightenment and Rousseau, the American Declaration of Independence of 1776 and the French Revolution, the Industrial Revolution, and finally the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948. Along the way, it argues, moral authority moved from revelation to human reason. The premises it identifies are a humanism that puts man at the centre, rationalism, individual free will, and a utilitarian ethics that judges actions by their social usefulness and practical results rather than by any divine command.

The authors give particular attention to Rousseau's Social Contract, including its claim that man is born free yet everywhere in chains, and his idea of the general will. They then turn to the social and political consequences: the rise of individualism and materialism, the weakening of family and community bonds, and the spread of Western cultural norms through globalisation, neo-colonial influence and “soft power”. They point to Oxfam figures on global wealth inequality, and to the veto held by a few states at the United Nations, to question how equally these rights work in practice.

The paper concludes that modern human rights carry the cultural assumptions of the societies that produced them, so their claim to universality should not be taken for granted. It calls for a more nuanced understanding that recognises their historical context and balances universal ideals with local values. It closes with the Qur'anic warning against becoming like those who forgot Allah, so that He made them forget themselves.
points: The paper traces modern human rights from the Renaissance to the 1948 Universal Declaration.
It argues their foundation is secular humanism, rationalism, free will and utilitarian ethics.
The authors link this framework to individualism, weaker families and the spread of Western norms.
They call for balancing universal ideals with local values rather than assuming universality.
human-rights-epistemological-basis.notes: The paper body is in Urdu and the PDF extraction is badly garbled; only the English abstract is fully readable. Paras 1, 2 and 4 follow the abstract closely. Details in para 3 and the ending were read from the garbled Urdu with reasonable but not full confidence: Rousseau's Social Contract and the 'born free, in chains' line, 1776 and the French Revolution, UDHR of 10 Dec 1948, Oxfam inequality figures (Latin-script 'Oxfam'), UN 'Veto Power' (Latin script), and the closing verse (appears to be Qur'an 59:19; number deliberately omitted). An Urdu reader should check these against the PDF before publishing. The paper is critical of secular human rights and Western influence; the summary attributes this to the authors. Blurb is accurate.
